passage: At the Friday review our new team lead, Alka, opened her arms wide and said, "Come on, tell me everything that is going wrong." I saw a few people lean in and smile. I am Jasleen, and I sit near the window. Alka's arms stayed open while Bhaskar spoke about the vendor delays, and she nodded and asked two questions. Later, when Mehul mentioned a similar problem, she checked her phone. Mehul's voice trailed off. I am not sure what Alka meant by the second glance, maybe an urgent message. The wide arms felt inviting, but I noticed the listening mattered more than the pose.

qa.q: Where does Jasleen sit?
qa.a: Jasleen sits near the window.

qa.q: What did Alka's open arms and questions suggest she felt, and what might her phone glance have meant?
qa.a: Alka seemed eager to hear honest input, since her arms stayed open and she asked Bhaskar two questions. The phone glance may have been an urgent message, but Jasleen cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Alka do to make her open posture match her listening?
qa.a: She could put her phone away in the review and keep asking follow-up questions, so the invitation feels real.

qa.q: How might Mehul have felt when Alka checked her phone?
qa.a: Mehul may have felt brushed off, since Mehul's voice trailed off after the glance.

grounding: Observer's account of a young leader spreading her arms to invite the team, where the effect depends on genuine listening.

passage:
Week 1. Jeevan, newly leading the sales group, spread his arms wide in the first meeting and said, "My door is open." People smiled, but nobody spoke. He talked for the whole hour.

Week 3. He tried it again, arms open, and this time added, "Rashmi, you have handled this client. What would you do?" She hesitated, then explained a problem in the pricing sheet. Jeevan took notes and did not interrupt.

Week 6. In the review Jeevan opened his arms and stayed quiet. Two juniors raised concerns, and Rashmi later thanked him for hearing them out. "You were listening this time," she said.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say in the first meeting?
qa.a: He said, "My door is open."

qa.q: Why did nobody speak in week 1, even though Jeevan's arms were open?
qa.a: He talked for the whole hour, so the open arms did not match his behaviour and gave people no room. The wide gesture could have been seen as welcoming, but he did not listen.

qa.q: What changed in Jeevan's approach that made people speak?
qa.a: He asked a direct question, stayed quiet and took notes without interrupting, which made the gesture real.

qa.q: How might Rashmi have felt in week 1 compared with week 6?
qa.a: In week 1 she might have felt unsure that speaking was welcome, while by week 6 she trusted that he would hear her out.

grounding: Illustrates a young leader spreading the arms wide to invite the team, with real effect depending on genuine listening.

passage: Urmila, I watched you open your arms wide at your first team meeting today. Lovely. Let me, Aparna, tell you what I got wrong with that same move. When I first led the nursing roster team, I'd stand at the front, spread my arms and say, "Anything at all, tell me." Big smile. Then someone would start, and I'd jump in with the answer before they'd finished. After two months, nobody raised anything. One evening Sister Mercy stayed back and said, "Your arms say come in. Your mouth says I already know." That stung. At the next meeting I spread my arms, asked, and then sat down and kept quiet until each person finished. It felt slow and uncomfortable. But by the end, Anand had told us about a night-shift gap we'd missed for weeks.

qa.q: What did Sister Mercy say to Aparna?
qa.a: "Your arms say come in. Your mouth says I already know."

qa.q: How did Aparna feel when Sister Mercy said that?
qa.a: Aparna felt stung and a little ashamed, realising the open gesture had been undercut by the interrupting.

qa.q: What choice at the next meeting made the open arms mean something?
qa.a: Aparna asked, sat down and stayed quiet until each person finished, so the invitation came with real listening.

qa.q: How might the team have felt during those first two months?
qa.a: They likely felt unheard and discouraged, since the welcoming arms were followed by interruptions, so they stopped raising anything.

grounding: An elder recalls spreading the arms to invite the team as a young leader and learning the gesture only worked with genuine listening.

passage: The monsoon had flooded the lower loading bay, and Abhinav, three months into running the night shift, had twenty minutes to decide how to move the orders. The team huddled under the tin roof, rain hammering so loud he had to shout. He spread his arms wide. "I don't have the full answer. What do you see?" A few people glanced at each other; the last supervisor had done the same thing and then ignored everyone. Pradeep, the oldest loader, spoke first, but the rain swallowed his words. Abhinav didn't nod and move on. He stepped right up beside him, bent his head close and said, "Again, please." Pradeep repeated it: use the upper ramp and pass the smaller boxes hand to hand in a chain. Abhinav turned back to the group. "Pradeep's plan. Let's go." They moved faster than he had ever seen.

qa.q: How long did Abhinav have to decide how to move the orders?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: What might Pradeep have felt when Abhinav bent close and said 'Again, please'?
qa.a: Pradeep probably felt respected and heard, maybe surprised too, since the last supervisor had invited ideas and then ignored everyone.

qa.q: What made Abhinav's open-arms invitation work?
qa.a: He followed it with genuine listening, moving close to hear Pradeep over the rain, and then actually used the plan.

qa.q: What would have changed if Abhinav had nodded and moved on when the rain drowned Pradeep out?
qa.a: The team would have seen the gesture as empty, like the last supervisor's, and might have stopped offering ideas.

grounding: Shows a young leader spreading the arms to invite the team under pressure, with the effect depending on genuinely listening.

passage: "Floor's open, everyone," Thomas said at the Friday huddle of his little bakery in Fort Kochi, arms spread wide over the flour-dusted counter. He liked this part; it made him feel like the kind of boss he'd always wanted to be. Pradeep, the morning baker, cleared his throat. "The new oven timer keeps resetting, and yesterday two trays of..." Thomas's phone buzzed. He glanced down and started typing a reply to a supplier, one arm still half open. Pradeep stopped mid-sentence. The others went very still. Thomas looked up into the silence and felt his face heat. "Sorry. That was rude." He put the phone face down on the shelf and folded his hands. "Two trays of what?" "Burnt," Pradeep said slowly. "Rusks. I think the timer's faulty." Thomas listened to the end, then wrote on the board: call the oven repair service, Monday.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say keeps resetting?
qa.a: The new oven timer keeps resetting.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when he looked up into the silence?
qa.a: Thomas felt embarrassed, his face heating, realising the open arms meant little while he was typing on his phone.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Checking the phone while Pradeep spoke made the invitation empty; putting the phone down, apologising and listening to the end repaired it.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt when Thomas started typing?
qa.a: Pradeep likely felt ignored and a bit foolish for speaking up, which is why he stopped mid-sentence.

grounding: Shows a young leader's spread-arms invitation undercut by not listening, then made real by attentive listening.

passage:
"Okay, team!" Nazia spread her arms wide at the head of the table. "This is an open floor. Any idea, any complaint, bring it!"
Amandeep raised a hand. "The weekend release keeps breaking. What if we shift to Tuesdays?"
"Hmm, no, weekends are fine. Next?"
Nobody else spoke.
Later, at the chai stall, Amandeep said, "Can I be honest, Nazia? The arms thing looked great. Very welcoming. But then you shut my idea in two seconds, and everyone saw."
Nazia winced. "I did, didn't I? I was so nervous about running my first meeting."
"Nervous is fine. Just, if you open your arms, open your ears too."
The following Monday, Nazia spread her arms again. When Amandeep spoke, she lowered them, sat down and said, "Tell me more. Why Tuesdays?"
Three people spoke after him.

qa.q: What did Amandeep suggest instead of the weekend release?
qa.a: Amandeep asked, "What if we shift to Tuesdays?"

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling during her first meeting?
qa.a: Nazia felt nervous about running a first meeting, which may be why she brushed off the idea so quickly despite the welcoming arms.

qa.q: What changed the following Monday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Nazia sat down and asked Amandeep to say more, so the open gesture was matched by real listening, and three more people spoke.

qa.q: How did the team experience the first meeting?
qa.a: They saw the open arms but also saw an idea shut down in seconds, so nobody else felt safe enough to speak.

grounding: A young leader's wide open arms invite the team, but the gesture only works when it comes with genuine listening.
